entries.title: add the secret-wipe and generated-golden rules to CLAUDE.md
entries.body:
Two rules from the security audit now sit in CLAUDE.md, where every session reads first.

Generated goldens are regenerated, never edited or merged by hand. `tests/self/goldens/checked.txt` and `checked-self.txt` are stage1's `--emit-checked` dump of the golden cases and of `src/`, so they move with any `src/` change and conflict with every open pull request that touches `src/`. Rewrite them only with `node tests/self/goldens.js --update`, and on a conflict merge `main` and regenerate.

Secret material in `std/crypto` is wiped once it can be. The runtime has no wipe primitive the optimiser cannot drop yet (#385). Until one ships, a function that holds a private key or a secret intermediate records it as unwiped in its area's record. Once it ships, every such function wipes before it returns, with a test that the wipe survives `-O2`.

A new Security section also points at SECURITY.md and docs/security/. The pull request also carries the v0.16.0 package-lock.json from the release's lockfile pull request (#392).

entries.title: build the wasi profile against a libc without realpath
entries.body:
The wasi-libc that Ubuntu and Debian package predates wasi-libc's
`realpath`. It neither declares nor defines the function, so with
`WASI_SYSROOT=/usr` every `--profile wasi` link stopped at
`runtime-os.c`'s call to it. That included `web/`'s `nish.wasm`.

`nish_realpath` now answers NULL there: the "does not resolve" answer
every caller already handles. The test is whether `<dirent.h>` spells
`DT_SOCK`. wasi-libc#463 added `DT_SOCK` in the same change that declared
`realpath` (#473 defined it a month later, with no wasi-sdk release
between them), so wasi-sdk 22 and later still call the real `realpath`.

`docs/INSTALL.md` now says where the package puts its sysroot (`/usr`, not
`/usr/lib/wasi-sysroot`), and that `realpathSync` answers `null` with it.

entries.title: constant-time check plumbing (CT-14, CT-15), a narrower nish-cmp declaration, and record corrections
entries.body:
The `ct_asm` assembly check now names each refusal by the kind it expects.
Before, every `expect=` other than `load` was reported as "refused for a
conditional branch", so the `call` and `latency` seeds read as branches
(CT-14). Each spec now carries its `promise` from `ctSpecs`, built from
one table of kinds that the `ct-check` grammar also reads, so a kind it
accepts always has a name. `via=` callees are named too.

A clang without the aarch64 (or x86-64) target now fails the run instead
of turning that half of the check into counted skips that left `npm test`
green with a note (CT-15). There is one `ct_asm: clang targets <target>`
check per target, and the failure is reported once with clang's answer.
The wasm32 compile, which reads no branches, stays a counted skip.

`tests/nish-cmp.js` loses its four every-program declarations. Against
0.16.0, three covered nothing. The fourth, the `!tbaa` element-tag
declaration, was absorbing one unrelated difference. In the two
`crypto_x25519` link programs, the seed names the `std/crypto/x25519`
module's output file by its own install path
(`home_user_nish_build_seed_std_crypto_x25519.ll`), while HEAD writes
`std_crypto_x25519.ll`. The bytes are identical. That is the
own-package-root case nish-cmp already sets aside inside a file, so
`withoutOwnRootNames` now sets it aside in a file name too, with its own
self-check cases. Every program agrees with 0.16.0 and no declaration
admits a difference everywhere.

Security record corrections from #388:
- K1-6 is marked fixed except for `join`, linking #382.
- The "held by discipline only" list now says `ct_asm_k1_ct` and
  `ct_asm_k1_base64url` read copies of `ct.ts` and `base64url.ts`.
- CG-3 links #382, and CT-13 links #378.
- CLI-6 is marked fixed by RT-4.
- CT-14 and CT-15 are fixed, and the index counts and open table are
  updated to match.

SC-16 records immutable releases as on: v0.16.0 reports
`immutable: true`. Build provenance attestations stay open (#389).

entries.title: HKDF-Expand-Label for TLS 1.3 and QUIC
entries.body:
`nish/crypto/hkdf` gains `hkdfExpandLabelSha256` and `hkdfExpandLabelSha384`, RFC 8446 §7.1's HKDF-Expand-Label, written once so that TLS 1.3 and QUIC (RFC 9001 §5.1) share it. The label is given without its `"tls13 "` prefix, which the function adds, and the `HkdfLabel` struct is handed to the existing `hkdfExpandSha256/384` as `info`.

Every argument is the program's choice rather than the peer's, so an out-of-range one panics rather than answering `null`: a length outside 0 to 255, a label empty or longer than 249 bytes, a context longer than 255 bytes, or a secret shorter than HashLen.

The answers are pinned against every HKDF-Expand-Label step RFC 8448 §3 prints and all of RFC 9001 A.1, in both number modes, with SHA-384 and the largest accepted arguments checked against OpenSSL's TLS13-KDF. The K1 security record gains an addendum for the new functions.

entries.title: declare the HKDF-Expand-Label nish-cmp differences against 0.16.0
entries.body:
HKDF-Expand-Label (#398) added `hkdfLabel`, `hkdfExpandLabelSha256` and
`hkdfExpandLabelSha384` to `std/crypto/hkdf.ts`. Each compiler links its
own `std/`, so against the 0.16.0 seed the five existing HKDF programs'
`hkdf.ll` now carries the new functions and strings, and the ten new
`crypto_hkdf_expand_label*` programs are refused by the seed, whose
`hkdf.ts` has no such export. #398 was branched before #397 removed
nish-cmp's every-program declarations, which had absorbed these, so main
went red on both `nish-cmp` jobs.

None of the fifteen is a codegen difference: the 0.16.0 seed, given this
tree's `hkdf.ts`, writes byte-identical IR for all of them. Each now has
a narrow entry, one program and one file, naming the change that ships
it, as `std_pair_*` does, to go when the next release becomes the seed.

entries.title: type an object literal in an `I | null` context as the struct, not the union
entries.body:
An object literal whose contextual type is `E | null` was checked against
`E`'s fields, but the checker recorded `E | null` as the literal's own type.
The emitter looks up the struct a literal allocates by that type, found none
for the union, and stopped with an internal error (`unknown struct`, exit 70).
That hit a ternary arm beside `null`, a `return`, an arrow's concise body, a
declared nullable local, a parameter and a nullable field alike.

The literal is now typed as the struct `E` itself. An `E` already converts to
`E | null` as the same pointer, so every one of those contexts compiles with
no further change, and the ternary's arms meet in one `phi` of `%struct.E*`
and `null`.

The 0.16.0 release stops on each of the five new `obj_lit_nullable_*`
programs with that internal error, so each is declared to nish-cmp against
this change's own release-note subject.

entries.title: prove a literal receiver's slice in range so NL8002 stays quiet
entries.body:
`"abcdef".slice(1, 3)`, and the same call on a `const` bound to that
literal, no longer raise the NL8002 portability warning. The receiver is
six bytes long and both bounds are inside `[0, 6]`, so the native check
cannot fire and TypeScript's clamp cannot move them: both print `bc`.

The slice proof now knows the length of a receiver whose ASCII text the
program spells out: a string literal, a `const` local bound to one (or
copied from such a `const`), and a module constant folded to one. A bound
is proven when it is a decimal literal at most that length, or a local the
bounds walk holds between 0 and that length. The receiver must be ASCII, so
its byte length and its UTF-16 length are the same number.

With two bounds, the literal proof also needs `start <= end`, from the
largest value the start can have and the smallest the end can have, so
`"abcdef".slice(5, 2)`, which panics natively where TypeScript answers
`""`, still warns. The ordering applies only where the literal length is
what proves a bound; a pair the existing length facts prove is judged as
before, and every warning still names the bound that fails.

The length is read only on the `slice` path, never as a `State` fact. The
shared `substring` proof is unchanged, so no emitted clamp moves and no IR
golden changes.

entries.title: remaining runtime hardening (RT-10..RT-13) and shim O_NOFOLLOW parity
entries.body:
The last four open findings of the runtime audit are closed, and the Node
twin now refuses a symbolic link where the native runtime does.

- **RT-10** `signalFd()` keeps both ends of its pipe in one 64-bit word and
  publishes them with one compare-and-swap. Two first calls that overlap
  answer the same descriptor, the one the handler writes to, and the pipe
  that lost is closed instead of leaking.
- **RT-11** `console.log`, `write` and the panic messages finish a short
  write instead of silently dropping the rest of the line.
- **RT-12** The descriptors `readFileSync*`, `writeFileSync` and
  `appendFileSync` open are close-on-exec, so a child another thread spawns
  does not inherit them.
- **RT-13** A `pread` or a file `write` that a signal interrupts is retried.
  A read used to hand back the bytes so far as the whole file, and a write
  used to fail with `cannot write`.
- `runtime/shim.mjs` opens `writeFileSync`, `appendFileSync` and
  `spawnSyncTo`'s streams with `O_NOFOLLOW`, as `runtime-os.c` does (RT-4).
  `nish.d.ts` says so, and `src/runtime.ts` notes where `willreturn` is the
  approximation CG-8 records.

Every unit stays inside its `.text*` ceiling: `nish_die` writes with `fputs`,
`getenv` and `realpathSync` share one copy into the arena, and a spawn
always builds its list of file actions.

entries.title: refuse push and pop on typed arrays reached through Map/Set reads, generics and imported aliases
entries.body:
WP33 R2 refused `push` and `pop` on a receiver spelled `Int32Array`,
`Float32Array`, `Float64Array` or `BigInt64Array` (NL2415), but three
shapes still compiled and pushed natively while the same source throws a
`TypeError` under Node. Each is now refused:

- **Another module's `type` alias.** A return type or a field written as
  `Samples`, where another module declares `type Samples = Float64Array`,
  is spelled where it is declared, the one module whose aliases the
  annotation names, and kept on the signature (`FunctionSig.returnSpelling`)
  and the field (`FieldInfo.spelling`). A caller reads that, so
  `make(2).pop()` is refused even in a module that never imports the alias.
- **A read out of a `Map`.** `Map<string, Float64Array>`, annotated, made
  with `new Map<…>()` or declared as a field, spells its values: `m.get(k)`
  once narrowed, `m.get(k) ?? d` and the variable of a `for...of` over
  `m.values()` carry the name. A `Set` holds no arrays, since an array is
  not a key.
- **A generic function's `T` result.** `first(rows)` with
  `first<T>(xs: T[]): T` and `rows: Float64Array[]` binds `T` to the
  argument's spelling at the call site, not on the instantiation: an
  `f64[][]` argument is the same instantiation and is not refused.

The change is compile-time only: no `.ll` golden moves and `sameType`
still holds, and the new spelling loops are guarded where the bounds
prover reads them, so the performance ratchet is unchanged. A member of a
generic class instantiated at a name, `new Box<Float64Array>(t).value`, is
the residue that remains, and docs/LANGUAGE.md says so.

entries.title: exercise nish:net's dual-stack IPv6 path, and correct its error-rule wording
entries.body:
`nish:net` binds `"::"` as an IPv6 socket with `IPV6_V6ONLY` off, and falls
back to IPv4's `0.0.0.0` on a kernel without IPv6. Until now only the fallback
had been run, because the containers the suite ran in have no IPv6. The new
case `net_dual_stack` listens on `"::"`, and the `net_` block of
`tests/run.js` connects to it from Node over `127.0.0.1` and then over `::1`.
The program must name the first peer in its mapped form and the second as
`::1`, each with Node's own port, and echo both. Its `"::"` UDP socket then
sends itself a datagram with each ECN mark over each family, so the mark
leaves as `IP_TOS` and as `IPV6_TCLASS`, and it must read every mark back from
`meta[1]`. CI's `ubuntu-latest` has IPv6 and runs the real path.

A host without IPv6 prints why and counts the check as a pass, not a skip:
there `"::"` is the documented fallback, not a gap. Only EAFNOSUPPORT (no
IPv6 in the kernel) and EADDRNOTAVAIL (IPv6 with no `::1` on loopback) count
as that; any other error on the probe fails the check and names its code,
and a self-check pins which codes go which way.

The `nish:net` rules in `docs/LANGUAGE.md` and the header of
`runtime/runtime-net.c` said errors follow "the same convention `signalFd`
set". They follow its shape, a negative `i32` for a failure, and add the
errno, where `signalFd` and `readSignal` answer a plain `-1`. Both now say so.
They also say plainly that on Darwin `meta[1]` is always `0`, which reads the
same as a real Not-ECT arrival, so a program learns that ECN is unsupported
from the `-95` of a marked send and never from a receive. No runtime code
changes.

entries.title: a secure-wipe builtin the optimiser cannot drop
entries.body:
`secureZero(bytes: u8[]): void` sets every byte of a `u8[]` to zero in
stores no optimisation may remove, which is what `std/crypto` needs to
clear a private key, a secret scalar or another secret intermediate once
it is used (ECC-2, X509-7). A plain `fill(0)` or `memset` before a key's
life ends is a dead store at `-O2`, and every program is linked with
`-flto`, which inlines a runtime `memset` into that caller and drops it
the same way. Non-escaping arrays live in the frame, so this is the
common case, not a corner.

The builtin is one call to `nish_wipe` in `runtime/runtime.c`, which
stores each byte through a `volatile` pointer and is `noinline`. Volatile
stores are behaviour the C standard keeps whatever the optimiser can see,
so they hold after LTO inlines the body too; the call is declared
`nounwind willreturn` and `nocapture` without `readonly`, with no memory
attribute that would let LLVM treat it as a store it may drop. The
checker takes a `u8[]` only, refuses a `readonly u8[]`, a value position
and a write inside a scope's region, as it does for
`crypto.getRandomValues`. Under Node the prelude supplies the same
zeroing loop.

The runtime unit test builds a probe with `-O2 -flto` over the runtime's
sources: a key written to a block, used, wiped, freed and read back
through a pointer the optimiser cannot follow. With no wipe, and with a
`memset` wipe in another translation unit, all 48 observed bytes still
hold the key; with `nish_wipe` none do, and the same test fails when
`nish_wipe` is written as a `memset`.

`std/crypto` does not call it yet: under the rolling freeze it may once
a release ships the builtin, and the security records say so.

entries.title: nish:net tcpConnect — the client half of TCP
entries.body:
A Nish program can now be a TCP client. `nish:net` gains two calls, each
also a global like the other sixteen.

`tcpConnect(addr: readonly u8[]): i32` creates a non-blocking,
close-on-exec socket and starts a `connect` to an 18-byte address, using
`AF_INET` for an IPv4 address and `AF_INET6` for any other. It returns the
descriptor at once, while the connection is still being made: the
`EINPROGRESS` of a non-blocking `connect` is not a failure, and the
readiness loop reports the descriptor writable when the connection
finishes. Any other failure closes the socket and is returned instead. An
address shorter than 18 bytes is -22.

`connectResult(fd: i32): i32` reads `SO_ERROR` once the descriptor is
writable. It answers 0 when the connection is made, or the negative
errno: -111 for a refused port, -110 for a timeout. The kernel clears
`SO_ERROR` as it is read, so a second call answers 0.

Neither call waits or allocates, so both are `willreturn`. On Darwin,
`ECONNREFUSED` and `ETIMEDOUT` are translated to Linux's numbers.
`nish_net_sockaddr` is now `noinline`, shared by three callers, which
keeps `runtime-net.c` under its existing `.text*` ceiling without
raising it.

This lands the first item of #357. Batching, edge-triggered mode, timers,
DNS, Windows and WASI stay open there.

entries.title: add using a = arena(), a checked arena bracket
entries.body:
A block that declares `using a = arena()` marks the arena where the
declaration stands and releases to that mark on every exit of the block:
its end, a `return` (after the returned value is computed), a `break` or
`continue` that leaves it, a `break` out of a `switch`, and an
`orReturn()`. The releases share the stack `using s = scope()` already
uses, so they nest with a scope's join, a loop pass's scope and a
function's automatic scope.

The compiler proves the release safe, which `Arena.release` never did. It
holds the block to the rule the compiler's own per-pass scopes are held
to, and refuses the block rather than quietly dropping the bracket. From
the declaration to the block's end, nothing allocated may be:

- assigned to a local declared outside (NL2418);
- stored into a field (NL2419), an element (NL2420) or memory any other
  way (NL2421);
- pushed onto an older array (NL2422), which also covers growing that
  array's buffer;
- returned or propagated by `orReturn()` (NL2423);
- kept by a callee (NL2424).

Arena control inside the block (NL2426) and a `spawn` on a scope declared
outside it (NL2427) are refused too. Each message names the value and
where it would escape to.

`arena()` anywhere but a `using` initialiser (NL2416) and any read of its
binding (NL2417) are refused. A parallel body or task may not open one
(NL2351). `using` accepts `arena()` beside `scope()`, with NL2387 and
NL2393 reworded.

`arena()` is a global builtin declared `declare function arena():
Disposable` in runtime/nish.d.ts, so a program stays TypeScript. Under
Node its disposal does nothing. A function that opens a block keeps its
automatic scopes.
metrics: 20000 passes that each grow a 1000-element array in a function with no automatic pass scope peak at 163,936 kB RSS without the block and 5,416 kB with it

entries.title: add `Secret<T>`, key material the checker keeps in and wipes
entries.body:
`nish:secret` holds a key as a `Secret<T>` — an array of integers or a
record of integer fields — and the checker refuses every road out of the
program but one. A `Secret` cannot be interpolated, printed, handed to any
builtin (files, sockets, processes, the environment, entropy), compared with
anything but another `Secret` or `null`, branched on, indexed or used as an
index, read into, built with `new`, or stored in a field, an array element, a
`Result` or a class's type argument. Each refusal has a code of its own,
NL2428 to NL2453, and is asked before the general rule the program would also
break, so the one diagnostic names the secret.

The one road is `expose(s, f)` and `exposeWith(s, arg, f)`. `f` is a function
parameter, judged once the whole-program facts are in: it may reach no I/O,
no clock, no entropy and no C at any depth of calls, and no `panic` or exit
whose message or status it computes; it keeps nothing of the value, writes
nothing through the argument `exposeWith` hands it, and declares a result
type that holds no `Secret`. That result is what leaves.

A `Secret` a function makes leaves it returned or wiped **on every path**.
This is Result rule 1's analysis in its two places, the statement that drops
a value and the body that never handles one, with the second walked path by
path rather than counted: a `wipe` on one arm of an `if` is not a wipe, and
every `return`, `break`, `continue` and `orReturn()` is an exit it checks.
A wiped `Secret` is not read again, `const j = k` moves `k`, and
`secret(local)` moves the local, which is not read again either.

`wipe` is one `llvm.memset` with its volatile flag set, over an array's whole
capacity or a record's `sizeof`, written by the emitter as the body of each
instance. Its facts say what that body does, so no parameter it writes is
`readonly`. `tests/run.js` holds it under `opt -O2` beside a twin whose
`fill(0)` of the same dead bytes is deleted outright: the twin keeps no
store, the wipe keeps one volatile zero per byte. `secureZero` (#417) stays
the global for a bare `u8[]`; key material belongs in a `Secret`.

`nish:secret` is the one builtin module with source behind it, `std/secret.ts`,
imported only by the builtin name and copied into each module that uses it,
as `std/collections.ts` is, so it writes no `.ll` of its own. `runtime/nish.d.ts`
declares it for `tsc`, and under Node `runtime/nish.mjs` resolves it to the
shim, where a `Secret` is a plain wrapper and `wipe` zero-fills it.

`std/crypto/p256.ts`, `x25519.ts` and `x509.ts` take and give private keys as
`Secret<u8[]>` and wipe every intermediate the key reaches: the key's limbs,
the nonce and its inverse, RFC 6979's `K` and `V` (whose HMAC is now written
out over `Sha256` so its key blocks and hasher state can be wiped), the nonce
point, the scalar multiply's table and accumulator, X25519's clamped scalar
and ladder, and every DER block decoded from a PEM key. ECC-2 and X509-7 are
closed; what a wipe cannot reach — a scalar in a register, the caller's PEM
string — is recorded in their audit records.

BREAKING CHANGE: `p256PublicKey`, `p256Sign` and `p256SignSha256` take the
private key as a `Secret<u8[]>`; `x25519` takes the scalar as one and answers
the shared secret as `Secret<u8[]> | null`; `x25519Base` takes the scalar as
one; `x509ParseP256PrivateKey` answers `Secret<u8[]> | null`, and
`x509MintSelfSigned` takes one. Wrap a key with `secret(bytes)`, read a result
with `expose`, and `wipe` what you made.

entries.title: carry a machine-applicable fix on a diagnostic, and apply it with nish --fix
entries.body:
A diagnostic printed by `nish --json` may now end with a `fix` key: a list of edits, `{"line","column","endLine","endColumn","text"}`, placed exactly as the diagnostic's own span is (1-based, columns in UTF-16 code units, the end exclusive). A span whose start equals its end is an insertion. The key is absent rather than empty when there is no safe rewrite, so every line without a fix is byte-identical to before. A fix is attached only when it keeps the program's meaning.

`nish --fix <files>` applies them. It rewrites only files named on the command line (never the standard library or a dependency), drops a fix that overlaps an earlier one, and recompiles until a round applies nothing or five have. Then it reports what is left exactly as a plain run would, `--json` included, with that run's exit code. It writes no IR, so `-o`, `--link` and the other product flags are a usage error (exit 2).

Loose equality is the first fix: `==` becomes `===` and `!=` becomes `!==`, replacing the operator token alone.
metrics: `--fix` on tests/fix/eq-multi-round takes 3 rounds (4 compiles) in 4 ms, against 3 ms for one plain compile

entries.title: report the capabilities each function, module and package can reach
entries.body:
Every builtin now carries exactly one capability label, or a deliberate none,
in a total audit table (src/capabilities.ts): clock, entropy, env, exit, ffi,
fs.read, fs.write, net, process.spawn and signal, with unsafe reserved for
nish:unsafe. A call to a `declare function` is ffi. The attribute pass carries
a capability mask and a shortest witness chain per capability over the whole
program's call graph, per generic instantiation and per function-parameter
instance, across packages. Ties go to the earlier call in the source, so the
report is byte-stable.

`--emit-capabilities <file.json>` writes the report: the program's set, whether
it is deterministic (it reaches none of clock, entropy, env, ffi, fs.read,
fs.write, net and process.spawn), and each package, module and exported
function with its set and a witness chain per capability. Keys come in a fixed
order, arrays are sorted, and paths are relative to the entry's directory.
`nish run --capabilities` prints one line on stderr before the program runs,
`capabilities: fs.read (not deterministic)`, and leaves its stdout alone.

An unlabelled builtin is an internal compiler error when the walk meets one,
and tests/capabilities.js fails the suite the day a builtin is added without a
row. Nothing is enforced yet; the enforcement is the next work package.

entries.title: nish/net/tls — the TLS 1.3 server handshake, reproducing RFC 8448 §3
entries.body:
`nish/net/tls` is a TLS 1.3 server handshake written as a pure state
machine: bytes in, records and events out, with no sockets. Fed the
client's flight from RFC 8448 §3, it produces the server's flight byte for
byte, and the handshake and application traffic secrets match the trace.

It negotiates TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 over x25519, sends a HelloRetryRequest when
the client offers no usable share, and chooses the version from
supported_versions alone. It signs CertificateVerify with ECDSA P-256. The
RFC 8448 trace is signed with RSA-PSS, so for that trace the test checks
the content to be signed and injects the trace's signature.

The parser bounds every length-prefixed vector by its own end, at every
nesting level: the extensions, each extension, and the lists inside
key_share, server_name and ALPN. A malformed hello gets decode_error and
the exact message, and never a panic.

The ephemeral key and the ECDHE secret are a `Secret` (#418) while they
are used, and both are wiped on every path. What stays unwiped, the
traffic secrets the caller receives as plain bytes, is recorded as TLS-1
in docs/security/tls.md.

entries.title: add nish:unsafe and scope the unsafe flags to the entry package
entries.body:
`--unchecked-indexing` and `--wrapping` used to reach every module of a
program, dependencies and the `nish/` standard library included, so one flag
on a command line made every out-of-range index anywhere undefined behaviour
and nothing in the source said so. This adds `nish:unsafe`, a builtin module
whose five functions state the same decisions at one site:

- `uncheckedGet(xs, i)` and `uncheckedSet(xs, i, v)` on an array of numbers
  with an `i32` index lower to the load and store `xs[i]` lowers to, with no
  `len` load, no compare and no branch to the bounds panic.
- `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` and `wrappingMul` on two `i32`s or two `i64`s
  are `add`, `sub` and `mul` with no `nsw`, whatever the command line says,
  and fold wrapping in a module constant.

A call reaches them only through `import { ... } from "nish:unsafe"`: the
global spelling `tsc` also accepts is refused (NL2456), so every module that
gives up a check or defines a wrap says so at its top. Each import and each
call site is recorded on the checked program and printed by
`--emit-checked`, for a capability report to read. Wrong arity, a non-numeric
receiver (NL2455), an `f64` index, mixed widths and unsigned operands
(NL2454) are refused; `runtime/nish.mjs` answers the import, so the same
program runs unmodified under Node.

The two flags now reach only the entry package's modules, never a
`node_modules` dependency or a `nish/` module, and each prints a deprecation
warning naming its replacement (NL9014, NL9015), under `nish run` too;
`--no-warn-performance` silences it. They are removed in a later release.
The `ct_asm_*` fixtures, which used `--unchecked-indexing` as a means, now
index through `uncheckedGet` / `uncheckedSet`, and their asm-checked
functions lower to the same IR as before.
metrics: 1.06x on a cache-resident gather loop, `xs[idx[k]]` vs `uncheckedGet(xs, idx[k])` (median 430 ms vs 406 ms over 9 runs, checksum -1447333761 both ways)

entries.title: builtins for the owner checks, and a cryptographic run-cache name (CLI-8)
entries.body:
Three builtins reach the RT-9 primitives `runtime/runtime-host.c` already
carries, so that the next release can let `src/` ask who owns a path and
whether it runs before trusting it (#386, CLI-7 and CLI-9):

- `lstatOwnerModeSync(path: string): i64` is one `lstat`, so a symbolic link
  answers for itself: the owner's uid in the high 32 bits and `st_mode` in the
  low 32, or -1 when the path does not resolve or holds a NUL. One call, so the
  owner and the mode always describe the same file.
- `geteuid(): i64` is the effective uid to compare that owner with.
- `isExecutableSync(path: string): boolean` is `access(path, X_OK)`, the
  shell's question, where a readable file is not the same answer.

Each lowers to one call, `i64` in both number modes because a uid fills 32
bits, ordered with every write as `statMtimeSync` is. They are refused on
wasm32, where `runtime-host.c` is empty, and supplied under Node by
`runtime/nish.mjs`, which prints the same lines for `owner_checks`. Under the
rolling freeze `src/` does not call them yet; CLI-7 and CLI-9 adopt them in the
release after this one.

Take the owner apart with `(om >> 32) & 0xffffffff`: a uid of 2^31 or more
fills bit 63 of the packed `i64`, so a plain `>>` would answer a negative
owner that never equals `geteuid()`. The builtins carry capability labels:
`fs.read` for `lstatOwnerModeSync` and `isExecutableSync`, `env` for
`geteuid`.

`nish run` now names each cache entry by the SHA-256 of its key instead of a
64-bit FNV-1a (CLI-8), and fingerprints the runtime files in the key the same
way. A hit still compares the whole key, so a collision never ran the wrong
program; a cryptographic name means two programs no longer share an entry at
all. The hash is FIPS 180-4 written in plain Nish in `src/run-cache.ts`,
because `src/` reads nothing from `std/`, and it agrees with `sha256sum` at
every padding boundary. Existing cache entries are simply not found again and
are rebuilt once.

`scripts/bootstrap.sh` keeps its stages in `<work>/bin/` and gives `<work>` the
checkout's `scripts`, `runtime` and `std` as symbolic links by absolute path,
so every stage finds the checkout through its own path instead of through the
compiler's working-directory fallback. A `--work` outside the checkout, which
failed at stage2 with `cannot find scripts/build.sh`, now builds and verifies.
metrics: SHA-256 hashes a 20 MB key in 138 ms where FNV-1a took 50 ms (about 145 vs 400 MB/s), clang 18.1.3, linux-x64

entries.title: close CG-2, CG-3, CG-4, CG-8 and CG-10
entries.body:
Closes the five codegen findings the security audit left open (CG-2, CG-3, CG-4, CG-8 and CG-10, tracked in #382). Each is fixed in its own commit and pinned by a regression test that fails on the base commit and passes after. `docs/security/codegen.md` and the index in `docs/security/README.md` now record all five as fixed.

- **CG-8:** the runtime calls that can exit or block are no longer declared `willreturn`. That covers `nish_read_file`, `nish_read_file_or_null`, `nish_read_file_bytes`, `nish_write_file`, `nish_append_file`, `nish_str_concat` and `nish_alloc_array`, and every caller loses it through the fixpoint. The allocator's own out-of-memory exit keeps it: only exits the program's input decides are counted.
- **CG-4:** `willreturn` is never inferred for a function on a call-graph cycle. A Tarjan walk clears it for self-recursion and for every member of a mutually recursive component before the fixpoint runs. Previously `opt -O2` deleted a non-terminating recursive `readnone` call, and a program that should hang exited 0.
- **CG-2:** `new Array<T>(n)` checks an `i32` `n` in both number modes. A negative length now panics with `array length out of range` before the inline allocator rounds it, where it used to wrap the rounding and `memset` until the process faulted.
- **CG-3:** `join` refuses a result longer than 2^31 - 1 bytes before allocating, failing as concatenation does (`nish: out of memory`, exit 1). Every source of a string or array is now bounded, so under `--number-mode i32` no `.length` can read back negative for the bounds prover to trust.
- **CG-10:** a compound element assignment whose right side may resize the array, as in `xs[0] += grow(xs)`, re-checks the index and re-takes the slot's address after the right side runs. The store lands in the array's current block, in JavaScript's evaluation order. Before this it stored into the old block (1 where Node prints 6).

A C host that links a module with a checked `new Array` length or a `panic` needs `runtime-os.c` (for `nish_exit`) as well as `runtime.c`.
metrics: join past the limit fails in 105 ms instead of answering a negative length after 4.5 s and ~2 GiB; tests/perf-baseline.json unchanged; nish-cmp declares 307 + 10 + 22 + 10 + 1 moved programs (CG-8, CG-4, CG-2, CG-3, CG-10), 0 undeclared

entries.title: fix truthiness, String(n), Map.get and call-site type arguments mechanically
entries.body:
The expression checker's mechanical rewrites now ride on the diagnostic as a
`fix`, which `nish --json` prints and `nish --fix` applies:

- A non-boolean condition becomes the comparison it meant under `tsc`:
  `!== 0` for an integer, `!== null` for a class or array that may be null,
  `.length !== 0` for a string, parenthesising the operand where it binds
  looser. A float (`NaN` is falsy) and `string | null` get no fix.
- `String(x)` and `n.toString()` become `` `${x}` `` when `x` is a number, a
  boolean or a string; a radix, a second argument, no argument or any other
  type gets none.
- `m.get(k)` held in a `let`, passed as an argument or used in arithmetic gets
  `?? 0`, `?? 0.0`, `?? ""` or `?? false`; a class, array, collection or
  nullable value type gets none.
- `f<T>(x)` and `h.get<T>(x)` lose the type argument when inference provably
  gives the type written: one parameter annotated `T`, and an argument that is
  a local of that type or a literal of it.
metrics: --fix on tests/fix/expr-truthy-number (6 edits, one rewrite) takes 5.0 ms median of 30, against 3.9 ms for the plain refused compile

entries.title: nish/net/quic-packet — QUIC packets, Initial secrets and header protection (WP34 Q1)
entries.body:
`nish/net/quic-packet` is QUIC v1's packet layer as pure functions (RFC
9000 §17, RFC 9001 §5). There are no sockets or connection state here.

It parses and builds long and short headers, together with the
variable-length integers and packet-number encoding they carry. A packet
number is decoded from its truncated form against the largest one seen
(RFC 9000 Appendix A), and never answers past 2^62 - 1. Initial secrets
come from the client's first destination connection id with the version
1 salt. Packet keys, IVs and header-protection keys come from a traffic
secret through HKDF-Expand-Label, and a key update derives the next
generation. Packets are sealed and opened with AES-128-GCM, and the
header is protected and unprotected with the AES-ECB mask. Retry packets
carry their integrity tag. Every value is checked against RFC 9001's
Appendix A vectors.

The traffic secrets and keys are plain arrays and are not wiped yet.
QUIC-1 in docs/security/quic.md records exactly what is left unwiped, and
#430 tracks moving the QUIC and TLS key-holding structs onto
`nish:secret`. That needs a key API redesign, which the connection stages
will consume. The security index's P-256/X25519 and X.509 rows, stale
since #418, are recounted.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: fix export default, export lists, type-only imports and fs imports mechanically
entries.body:
Four more refusals now carry a machine-applicable fix, so `nish --fix` applies them and `nish --json` prints the edit:

- `export default f` (NL2129) deletes the statement and writes `export ` before the declaration of `f`.
- `export { f, g }` (NL2128) deletes the list and writes `export ` before each declaration it names.
- `import type { T } from "./m"` (NL2243) loses its `type`.
- `import { readFileSync } from "fs"` (NL3015) becomes `from "nish:fs"`, when every name it imports is one `nish:fs` exports.

Each fix is all or nothing and is left out whenever it would not keep the program's meaning: `export =`, a default of anything but a bare name, a name that is imported, undeclared, declared twice or already exported, a `const` that binds a second name (which `export` would export too), a re-export (`export { f } from`, `export * from`, `export * as ns from`), a renamed or type-only entry, `import type T from` and `import type * as m from` (each still a refused import without `type`), and an `fs` import naming something `nish:fs` lacks.

The NL9007 range guard gets no fix. The only behaviour-preserving rewrite is `if (!(i >= 0 && i < xs.length)) { panic("...") }` before the statement, and the bounds analysis does not credit it: it ends a path at `return`, `break` and `continue` but not at `panic`, so the warning and the check would both stay. Wrapping the access in the guard instead would turn the panic into a silent skip.

`nish --fix` now also refuses a fix whose own edits overlap each other, which no order of applying them makes right (`export { f, f }` asks for `export ` before `f` twice). The case that pins it and the case that pins dropping one diagnostic's fix where an earlier one already edits the same span are the first to reach either branch.
metrics: `--fix` on tests/fix/decl-export-list (four declarations, one round) takes 3.4 ms against 2.5 ms for one plain compile, medians of 7

entries.title: nish/net/hpack — HPACK with Huffman (WP34 H2, first part)
entries.body:
`nish/net/hpack` is RFC 7541 in pure Nish and sans-IO. It implements the
§5.1 integer with an N-bit prefix, the §5.2 string literal with Appendix
B's Huffman code, the 61-entry static table, the dynamic table with size
updates and eviction, and all four representations, behind an
`HpackEncoder` and an `HpackDecoder` per connection direction.

The Huffman code is stored as its 257 code lengths. Appendix B's code is
canonical, so the lengths determine every code, and the test checks each
code against the appendix. The encoder takes the representation and the
Huffman choice per field. It sends a never-indexed field as a literal even
when a table holds it.

The decoder refuses each of the following with a sticky negative code: a
truncated block, an integer past 2^31 - 1, an index of zero or out of
range, Huffman padding over seven bits or not all ones, EOS, and a size
update above the SETTINGS limit, after a field, or missing when a lowered
limit requires one. A header list over the caller's limit is still decoded
to its end, so the table stays in step, and is answered with a non-fatal
`HPACK_LIST_TOO_LARGE`. A field past that limit is counted from the
table's own arrays and never copied, so repeated indexes of a large entry
cannot allocate past it.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: record every panic site with its kind, and --emit-panics
entries.body:
A compiled program can stop with exit 1 in more places than the `panic`
calls its author wrote: a bounds check the checker could not prove away, an
integer division, a value entering `integer<Lo, Hi>`, `r.expect`, a
`readFileSync` of a missing file. The checker now records each of those as a
**panic site** with its kind, and `--emit-panics <file.json>` writes them
function by function, beside the IR and without changing a byte of it.

The kinds are `index`, `pop`, `slice`, `divide`, `range`, `array-length`,
`panic`, `expect`, `io-exit`, `parallel-length`, `call` and `oom`. A site is
listed exactly where the emitter writes a check that can fail, or calls into
the runtime where it exits, and is `"proven": true` where a proof table lets
the emitter leave the check out, so the file shows what the checker proved as
well as what it did not. This includes the checks #427 added: an i32 or
ranged `new Array(n)` length, and the index re-check of a compound store
whose right side makes a call. A call into a function that may panic is a
`call` site of the caller, naming the callee and the kind it reaches
(`"via"`), decided as a fixpoint over the whole program, the standard library
and dependencies included. `--unchecked-indexing` is not a proof: the access
it stops checking is still an unproven site. Out of memory is listed as `oom`
with `"allowed": true` and never makes a function one that may panic; stack
overflow and signed overflow (still `nsw`) are not sites at all.

The sites are recorded by the attribute walk in `src/attributes.ts`, beside
the line that already tells the fixpoint each construct reaches a `noreturn`
callee, and resolved once in `src/panics.ts` after `proveCallSiteRanges` and
`checkParallel`, over the attribute pass's own call graph. Nothing is
recorded unless the flag is given. `--emit-panics` is refused with
`--emit-ast` (which stops before the check), by `nish run` and by `--fix`,
and is written beside the `--emit-checked` dump.

`npm test` holds the list to the IR: every golden in `tests/cases/` is
compiled again with the flag and its IR must be byte-identical, and there and
in every program in `tests/link/` a function whose sites are all proven (or
`oom`) must have no `nish_panic_*` call, no panic tail and no exiting runtime
call in its IR. A function the file lists for the module being checked but
the IR does not define is a failure, so a drifted symbol cannot pass in
silence. The rule is "Panic sites" in docs/LANGUAGE.md.
metrics: compiling src/compile.ts (77 modules), median of 11 interleaved runs, both compilers built by one seed: 1211 ms before, 1161 ms after without the flag (noise; nothing is recorded), 1225 ms with --emit-panics (2236 functions listed); IR byte-identical

entries.title: deprecate Arena.release and Arena.reset in favour of using a = arena()
entries.body:
`Arena.release` and `Arena.reset` are the one place left where ordinary code can reach undefined behaviour in the arena: releasing while anything allocated after the mark is still referenced reuses that memory. `using a = arena()` does the same release with the proof done by the compiler. Every call to the old two now prints a deprecation warning that points to it. They still compile and run, and `Arena.mark` and `Arena.used` are unchanged.

Deprecation is a new warning class beside performance and portability:

- It prints by default as `file:line:col: deprecation: …`, and no flag silences it.
- `--json` carries it as `severity: "deprecation"` under code NL7001, the first code of a new NL7xxx band. `gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs` checks that band like NL8 and NL9.
- It never changes an exit code, and it is dropped when the program fails to check, as performance warnings are.
- It is reported the same way under `--fix` and `nish run`.
- A call inside a generic function warns once per call site, not once per instantiation.

The NL9011 arena-loop advice now recommends `using a = arena()` instead of `Arena.mark()` and `Arena.release(m)`. The repo's own loop-scope tests use the new bracket. The tests that exist to exercise the old API keep it and pin the warning. `std/` and `examples/` call neither.
metrics: 2 repo programs migrated to `using a = arena()` (mem_loop_scope, mem_loop_scope_forof); 0 deprecation warnings across std/ and examples/

entries.title: nish/net/http1 and nish/net/websocket — the HTTP/1.1 parser and RFC 6455 framing (WP34 H1)
entries.body:
`nish/net/http1` is an incremental, sans-IO HTTP/1.1 request parser after
RFC 9112. It reads the request line, header fields and a body framed by
Content-Length or chunked transfer coding. Every limit is the caller's:
line, header-field count and size, and body. It refuses with a sticky
status what the RFC refuses: bare CR, obs-fold, a Content-Length together
with Transfer-Encoding, conflicting lengths, a chunk size with trailing
whitespace and no extension, and an overlong method or target fed in
pieces. It also writes responses.

`nish/net/websocket` is RFC 6455's server side: the opening-handshake key
check and accept value (on a new `nish/crypto/sha1`, used only for this
and checked against RFC 3174's vectors), and frame parsing and building
with masking, fragmentation, control-frame limits, and close codes and
reasons. Every RFC 6455 example frame is reproduced byte for byte.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: nish/net/tls records over TCP (WP34 T2)
entries.body:
TLS 1.3 now runs over TCP. Three new modules sit around `nish/net/tls`'s
handshake.

- `nish/net/tls/record` is the record layer of RFC 8446 §5. It frames a
  stream into records in a buffer allocated once. It seals and opens each
  record under a traffic secret: the nonce comes from the sequence number,
  the header is the additional data, and the inner content type and zero
  padding are found without branching on the padding. It also derives
  KeyUpdate's next secret.
- `nish/net/tls/record-server` runs a `TlsServer` over a byte stream,
  sans-IO. It sends the flight as one record once it is signed, installs
  every key at the record boundary §5.1 puts it on, sends the compatibility
  change_cipher_spec of §D.4, handles alerts both ways, and does KeyUpdate
  both ways and on a schedule.
- `nish/net/tls-tcp` puts it on `nish:net` for a program that owns its
  loop. A pool of slots is sized at start-up. Every call answers the slot's
  interest, whose low bits are `pollModify`'s events.

After its handshake a connection allocates nothing per record. A key install
leaves HKDF's and the AES schedule's temporaries in the arena (5,248 bytes),
because `Arena.release` is deprecated and a `using a = arena()` block is
refused while those callees store allocations. So a connection takes at most
64 KeyUpdates from its client and refuses the 65th with `unexpected_message`.
RFC 8446 §4.6.3 sets no such limit, so a client that updates on a clock of its
own is disconnected at its 65th: a deliberate trade-off that TLS-3 records.
On this path `TlsServer`'s traffic and handshake secrets, the ephemeral key
and every per-record nonce are wiped with `secureZero` once they are no longer
needed.

RFC 8448 §3's nine records are reproduced byte for byte, both by the record
layer and over a socket, and the client's stream is replayed at every cut
point. openssl s_client (under all three suites, and with a KeyUpdate) and
curl interoperate from tests/run.js. docs/security/tls.md records what is
still open:

- TLS-2: the AES schedule's wipe.
- TLS-3: the memory each handshake leaves behind, and the KeyUpdate cap.
- TLS-4: the carrier has no timeout.

Measured: 0 arena bytes over 200 echoes; 10,496 bytes per answered KeyUpdate, 671,744 at the 64-update cap; about 52 KB per handshake (peak RSS, 1,000 to 4,000 handshakes)
Refs: docs/security/tls.md, std/README.md, RFC 8446 §5, RFC 8448 §3
Tests: tests/link/net_tls_record_rfc8448, tests/link/net_tls_record_refusals, tests/link/net_tls_record_tcp, tests/link/net_tls_record_*_f64, tests/run.js net_tls_tcp

entries.title: nish/net/quic — QUIC connections, the handshake and stream data (WP34 Q2, first part)
entries.body:
`nish/net/quic` is the server side of a QUIC version 1 connection, sans-IO.
`QuicConnection` takes the datagrams a client sends and answers the ones to
send back. It has no socket, clock or random device of its own.

It drives `nish/net/tls`'s `TlsServer` over CRYPTO frames at the Initial,
Handshake and 1-RTT levels (RFC 9001 §4). Each level's packet keys come from
`nish/net/quic-packet` as soon as TLS knows the secret, and are discarded
and wiped when RFC 9001 §4.9 says.

The server's transport parameters go out in EncryptedExtensions and name the
original and initial connection IDs. The client's are parsed and checked
before the flight leaves (RFC 9000 §7.3).

Once connected:

- Every ack-eliciting packet is acknowledged in its space.
- The client gets new connection IDs once the handshake is confirmed.
- PATH_CHALLENGE is answered.
- A datagram with an ack-eliciting Initial is padded to 1200 bytes, and an
  unvalidated client is sent at most three times what it sent (§8.1).
- The client's stream data comes out of `readStream()` in order per stream,
  and `writeStream` queues a reply within the client's credit.

A protocol violation closes the connection with the transport error
RFC 9000 names, and a TLS alert closes it with CRYPTO_ERROR. A packet that
cannot be used is dropped and counted. A NEW_CONNECTION_ID refused for the
§5.1 limits leaves the connection-ID table exactly as it was.

Four modules beside it hold the parts, each tested on its own:

- `nish/net/quic-frame` reads every frame of RFC 9000 §19 and writes the
  ones a server sends.
- `nish/net/quic-conn-params` handles the transport parameters of §18.
- `nish/net/quic-conn-ack` holds the received packet numbers an ACK is
  written from.
- `nish/net/quic-conn-cid` is the connection-ID table.

Not here:

- Loss recovery (Q3).
- Flow-control updates and server-opened streams (Q4).
- Retry, Version Negotiation, stateless reset, the idle timer and key update
  (Q2b).

docs/security/quic.md records what is open. QUIC-2 is what a connection holds
between calls that no wipe reaches. QUIC-3 is its per-packet arena growth.

Measured: aioquic 1.3.0 completes a handshake and a stream echo against the server over loopback; the replay of that exchange from a Nish UDP client takes 4 ms, every server datagram byte for byte
Refs: docs/security/quic.md, std/README.md, RFC 9000, RFC 9001
Tests: tests/link/net_quic_frame, tests/link/net_quic_conn_parts, tests/link/net_quic_conn, tests/link/net_quic_conn_replay (each with an _f64 twin)

entries.title: nish/net/quic — Retry, version negotiation, stateless reset, idle timeout and key update (WP34 Q2, second part)
entries.body:
`nish/net/quic-listener` answers what a QUIC server sees before any
connection exists. `QuicListener.handle(datagram, address, now)` does three
things:

- It answers Version Negotiation for any version but 1 in a full-sized
  datagram, and never for version 0.
- It sends a Retry whose token is good for at most a minute. The token is
  an HMAC-SHA256 over the issue time, the original DCID, the Retry's SCID
  and the client's address and port. A forged, moved, expired or
  misdirected token closes the attempt with INVALID_TOKEN.
- It answers a short header to an unknown ID with a stateless reset that
  ends in the token the static key gives that ID. The reset is always
  shorter than what it answers, never under 21 bytes, and rate limited.

`nish/net/quic` now takes the caller's time: `receive(datagram, now)`,
`takeDatagram(now)`, `deadline()` and `handleTimer(now)`.

- **Idle timeout.** It is the smaller of both sides' `max_idle_timeout`,
  at least three probe timeouts, and it closes silently.
- **Key update, both ways.** The next read keys are derived ahead of time,
  so a forged Key Phase bit costs nothing. The client's updates are
  followed, and the server starts its own with `updateKeys()`. A client may
  start at most 64 updates a connection, which bounds what it can make the
  server derive (QUIC-4).
- **Stateless reset tokens.** Every connection ID now carries the token the
  configuration's static key gives it, the first one in the
  `stateless_reset_token` transport parameter.
- **Retry.** `acceptRetry` opens a connection the listener validated.

`release()` and the idle timeout wipe every key and secret the connection
holds. That includes both sides' stateless reset tokens and TLS's expected
client Finished.

Measured: each key update a client starts leaves 11,200 bytes in the arena (AES-128-GCM), capped at 64 a connection (716,800 bytes); a forged Key Phase bit costs 608 bytes and derives nothing; the five aioquic 1.3.0 scenarios replay in 12 ms
Refs: docs/security/quic.md, std/README.md, RFC 9000 §6, §8.1, §10.1, §10.3, RFC 9001 §6
Tests: tests/link/net_quic_lifecycle, tests/link/net_quic_lifecycle_replay (each with an _f64 twin), tests/link/net_quic_conn, tests/link/net_quic_conn_replay

entries.title: write down the builtin and mutation-check conventions, and bring the security records up to date
entries.body:
`.claude/selfhost.md` gains two conventions that contributors had been

entries.title: let the stage-1 fuzz differential declare an intended IR change, and run it in CI
entries.body:
`tests/differential/fuzz.js --stage1` compares the released seed's IR with
HEAD's over random programs, and until now it had no way to accept a
difference HEAD means to make. #427's CG-8 fix took `willreturn` from
`nish_str_concat`, so every seeded `npm test` failed with 15 disagreements
on seed 20261001 (#438), while CI, whose `test` job has no seed, saw nothing.

The fuzzer now has a `DECLARED` list of its own, the counterpart of
`tests/nish-cmp.js`'s. An entry names a function and its attribute group's
text on the seed side and on HEAD's, keyed by text rather than `#N` because
the numbers follow first use; it carries the `changelog` subject that made
the change and a `why`. A program whose only differences are declared ones
is reported as `declared` and passes, anything else still fails, and an
entry nothing in the run matches fails as stale, so the reseed after the
release retires it. Only `nish_str_concat` is declared: the other functions
CG-8 changed read files or build arrays, which no generated program does,
and 200 programs from seed 7000 differ nowhere else.

`tests/run.js` drives the matcher over fabricated modules on every run,
seed or not: an undeclared group change fails, a declared one passes (and a
module that also differs in an instruction does not), and a declaration
nothing matches is stale. CI's `nish-cmp` job now runs 200 programs from
the fixed seed against each released seed, reusing the candidate nish-cmp
just linked, which adds about 3 s per row. `.claude/testing.md` states the
rule: an intended IR change is declared wherever HEAD meets the seed.

Each entry's `changelog` words are checked as nish-cmp checks its own,
through its exported `isNamed` and `pendingNotes`, against `CHANGELOG.md`
and the release notes the unreleased commits render, so a mistyped or
never-shipped subject fails the run; the CG-8 entry carries the words as
the notes render them, "Close CG-2, CG-3, CG-4, CG-8 and CG-10". A
differing module must also refer to every attribute group it defines, so
an orphan group cannot ride along with a declared change.

Refs: #438, #427, .claude/testing.md
Tests: tests/run.js "fuzz --stage1: ..." self-checks, fuzz.js --stage1 --seed 20261001 --count 16

Closes #438

entries.title: make signed integer overflow a checked panic by default
entries.body:
Signed `i32` and `i64` arithmetic no longer assumes it cannot overflow. Every
`+`, `-`, `*`, unary `-`, `++`, `--` and `op=` on a signed integer is now one
of two things:

- **Proven to fit.** `src/bounds.ts` records the operation in a new per-node
  table, `nodeProvenNoOverflow`, and the emitter writes the plain instruction
  with `nsw`. Here the flag restates a proof rather than making an assumption.
- **Checked.** Everything else is lowered through
  `llvm.s{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow` and branches to one cold `ovf.fail`
  block per function. That block calls the new noreturn runtime entry
  `nish_panic_overflow`, which prints `attempt to add with overflow` (or
  subtract, multiply, negate) and exits 1, the way division by zero already
  does. Under `-g` each source location gets a block of its own, so a
  panic carries the location of the check that failed.

Before this change, the default put `nsw` on every signed operation, so an
overflow was poison and LLVM was free to fold `x + 1 > x` to `true`. A
TypeScript program that TypeScript accepts could therefore be compiled into
undefined behaviour. Under the new default an overflow panics.

The proofs come from the bounds walk's existing facts plus interval
arithmetic over them:

- a loop counter below an array length or an `i32` bound;
- a step whose operands are literals, constants, `.length`, masked or shifted
  values, or widened `toI64` conversions;
- `i * i <= n` against a known `n`;
- a bounded accumulation in a counted loop;
- an argument whose range is the same at every call site, through the
  `src/ranges.ts` fixpoint. That fixpoint now widens a fact that keeps moving
  after 16 rounds, so it still settles;
- what a function returns: a call to a plain function has the range of its
  returns, a `Result`'s `Ok` payload included, and `return r.value` hands on
  the range of the payload the caller passed. The summaries are gathered in
  the same fixpoint and are read only to judge an operation, so no fact or
  entry rests on them, and one that keeps changing is given up after 16
  moves.

The attribute fixpoint counts `nish_panic_overflow` as a callee for every
operation that keeps its check, so `willreturn` and the effect summary stay
sound.

`--emit-panics` lists every checked signed operation as an `overflow` panic
site, a new kind that takes the next free number. A site is marked proven where
the bounds walk proved it fits and the emitter writes `nsw` instead of the
check. No site is listed under `--wrapping` or for a `nish:unsafe` `wrapping*`
call. The IR oracle counts a call to `nish_panic_overflow` as a panic path, so
a report that left one out fails.

An operation meant to wrap is written `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` or
`wrappingMul` from `nish:unsafe`, which is never checked. The deprecated
`--wrapping` still makes every operator of the entry package wrap, and the
standard library and dependencies stay checked under it. `--nsw` is now
refused with exit 2 and a message that names both, so no flag brings the
undefined behaviour back.

On wasm the panic is declared `extern_weak`, and the WASI runtime's version
traps.

Code that relied on wrapping was rewritten in unsigned types rather than
built with `--wrapping`. In `std/crypto`, that is base64url, ct, the
ChaCha20-Poly1305 word reads, AES, P-256 and the X25519 limb arithmetic. The
constant-time fixtures under `tests/cases/ct_asm_*` mirror those rewrites. The
self-hosted compiler needed no such change: `scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify`
still reaches stage3 == stage2.

The runtime core's `.text*` ceiling rises by one byte to 3,606, because the
two panics share one table of messages (docs/wp7-runtime.md).

Every benchmark is within 5% of its base except three, and the project's
owner accepted all three as the cost of the rule:

- **fib** (+40% to +64% across machines). `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` can overflow, and the checked add
  keeps LLVM from turning the recursion into a loop with an accumulator.
- **awfy Permute** (+25% to +40% across machines). Its one check, `this.count += 1`, genuinely can
  overflow: nothing bounds how many times `permute` runs. The cost is how LLVM
  places the frame, because a conditional panic on the leaf path keeps the
  prologue ahead of the `n !== 0` test.
- **awfy Bounce** (+23% to +37% across machines). Proving its checks needs field ranges and a class
  invariant that holds between method calls: `this.x += this.xVel` is
  restored to range by the clamps that follow it. That analysis is left as
  follow-up work. Built with `--wrapping`, Bounce matches its base.

`bench/instructions.json` is raised to the counts measured on this change for
those three, and for the eleven programs that stay within 5% of their wall
time but move past the instruction tolerance: sieve, the seven map
benchmarks, Towers, Mandelbrot and Storage. No other entry moves.

A `call` site's `"via"` in `--emit-panics` is the kind its callee reaches
first at run time, its own checks and its calls taken together. The walk
numbers a node's sites after its operands', so `pick(xs, i) + 1`,
`1 + pick(xs, i)`, `x += pick(xs, i)` and `100 / pick(xs, i)` all reach
`pick`'s `index` first. A divisor that called a checked function reported
`divide` before this change, and now reports what the call reaches. Each
function's answer is settled once, so resolution terminates on call cycles.
In a cycle of calls made before any check, the cycle's first function in
declaration order with a site of its own or a call out of the cycle passes
over its calls back into it, and the rest of the cycle reaches what it
reaches.

Under `--deny-panics` and `noPanic` (#443), an unproven overflow site is
refused like any other panic site, with NL2457 and a hint that names the
unsigned type for its width and the operator's drop-in `nish:unsafe` form:
`wrappingAdd(x, y)`, `x = wrappingAdd(x, y)` for `+=`, `wrappingSub(0, x)`
for unary `-`, and `x = wrappingAdd(x, 1)` for `++`. A proven operation,
`--wrapping` and the `wrapping*` calls are accepted. The overflow panic kind
takes the next free number after #443's `unchecked`.

entries.title: let a nish:unsafe import opt uncheckedGet and uncheckedSet into the no-panic scope
entries.body:
Under `--deny-panics` or `"nish".noPanic`, `uncheckedGet` and
`uncheckedSet` were refused as `unchecked` sites, so a module that
needed an unchecked index had to leave the scope entirely. They cannot
panic: they have no check at all, and an index out of range is
undefined behaviour instead. A call to either is already accepted only
through `import { … } from "nish:unsafe"` at the top of its own module
(NL2456 refuses the global spelling, and re-exports are not supported),
so that import is the explicit, visible opt-in the work stream asks for.

An `unchecked` site is now allowed the way `oom` is. `--emit-panics` and
the `--emit-capabilities` `"panics"` list keep it, written with
`"allowed": true` in place of `"proven": false`. It never makes its
function one that may panic, so a call into such a function is not a
`call` site, inside the scope or out of it. That includes the NL2458
case: a listed module calling a dependency that uses `uncheckedGet`.

`--unchecked-indexing` is unchanged. It drops checks with nothing in
the source to show for it, so an index it left unchecked is still
refused. The IR oracle now treats any `"allowed"` site as one that
cannot panic, so every function whose only sites are `unchecked` is
also held to having no panic path in its IR.

No IR changes: `nish-cmp` against 0.16.0 reports 0 undeclared differences.
metrics: 0 bytes of IR changed across 1218 nish-cmp programs; a call into an unchecked-only function now has 0 call sites (1 before)

entries.title: refuse a program that reaches a capability its policy does not grant (WP36)
entries.body:
* feat(checker): refuse a program that reaches a capability its policy does not grant (WP36)

A program can now be held to the capabilities it is allowed. `--deny
<cap>[,<cap>...]` refuses a capability outright, and `--allow` turns the
policy into an allowlist; both repeat and take comma lists. The root
`package.json` says the same in `"nish": { "capabilities": { "allow": [...],
"deny": [...] } }`, beside `noPanic`. Denials union and allowlists
intersect, so the command line can only narrow what the package says.
Only the entry's closure is judged: `main`'s, or each export of a library.

A refused capability is NL2459, spanned at the first call of its witness
chain and naming every hop the way `--emit-capabilities` writes them. A
manifest policy the compiler cannot honour is refused where package.json
writes it: the wrong shape (NL3032), a name that is no capability
(NL3033), `unsafe` under `allow` (NL3034), a capability both allowed and
denied (NL3035). On the command line the same mistakes, and a
`fs.read=<dir>` scope that nothing enforces yet, are usage errors.

The reserved `unsafe` bit is wired: a call to a `nish:unsafe` export
carries it, so `--deny unsafe` refuses a program that gives up a check
anywhere in its closure. The import is the opt-in, so an allowlist never
refuses it and `--allow unsafe` is refused. No IR changes.

Measured: no .ll golden moves; src/compile.ts's performance-warning counts are unchanged against tests/perf-baseline.json
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#the-capability-policy, docs/wp36-capability-policy.md
Tests: tests/wordings/nl2459_*, tests/link/caps_policy_*, tests/nish/cli.ts checkCapabilityPolicy

* refactor(checker): read the root manifest once, and name the opt-in capabilities in one place

The simplify pass over the capability policy: the root package.json is read
once per compile for both noPanic and the policy, optInCapabilities() holds
the rule that unsafe is opted into by its import, and everyCapabilityName()
replaces the name list written twice. nish-cmp declares the new programs by
the words the release notes render.

* fix(checker): judge every function a host can call against the capability policy

Review round 1. The policy judged only `main`, or the entry module's
exports, so an open build — `-o` alone, a header or N-API sidecar, a
`declare function`, wasm — let a second module's export, or under
`--no-strict-exports` a private helper, reach a denied capability and
compile. What is judged is now exactly what `hostVisible` calls
host-visible for the build: `main` alone in a closed `--link` build, and
`main` plus every host-visible function of every module in an open one.
`main` is judged first, so a program's refusal names it wherever it is
declared.

A manifest entry's span is now the value as written, so a non-string entry
such as `123` is spanned without two phantom quotes. Tests pin the manifest
and command line together (the CLI cannot widen a denial, allowlists
intersect, `--deny` narrows an `allow`), a library entry, a private helper
under `--no-strict-exports`, a second root behind `--emit-header`, two
refusals in one compile as text and as `--json`, and the non-string span.

Measured: self-compile of src/ 2,001,256,663 instructions before and 2,001,305,198 after with no policy (+0.0024%), 2,003,685,892 with --deny net,signal (+0.12%), callgrind
Refs: docs/wp36-capability-policy.md
Tests: tests/link/caps_policy_cli_cannot_widen, caps_policy_allow_intersect, caps_policy_allow_narrowed, caps_policy_manifest_allow_cli_deny, caps_policy_two_denied, caps_policy_manifest_non_string; tests/wordings/nl2459_policy_library, nl2459_policy_unexported

* fix(checker): refuse a capability policy that writes allow or deny twice

Review round 2. A repeated `"allow"` or `"deny"` key inside
`"nish".capabilities` was read into the same list, so
`{"allow":["fs.read"],"allow":["exit"]}` granted `exit`: the two lists were
unioned and the policy widened. It is now NL3032, spanned at the second key,
since neither reading of it is safe — JSON.parse keeps the last, and
reading both widens.

Tests: tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_repeated

* fix(checker): prove every step of the capability-policy reader, so the self-build reaches its fixed point

`bootstrap (x86_64-linux)` and `(x86_64-darwin)` failed on this branch:
stage2's and stage3's IR were identical, yet their binaries differed. The
cause is that clang 18's `-O3 -flto` link of one fixed command and one
fixed set of inputs gave two different binaries about one run in three to
six. Every differing byte was in `Compilation.check`, where
`manifestCapabilities` is inlined. Its eight `llvm.s*.with.overflow`
checks — `i + 1`, `keyEnd - 1` and `colon + 1` on positions the bounds
walk could not bound — were proven away by LLVM on some runs and kept on
others. `main` at cad7114 does not trigger it.

The reader now tests every position against the text's length before it
steps past it, so each step is `nsw` with no check, and the function has
no overflow intrinsic left. The same link is then byte-identical over
eight runs, and `scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify` reports
`stage3 == stage2`.

Measured: 8 of 8 identical links of the stage2 IR, against 1 in 3 to 6 differing before; manifestCapabilities' overflow checks 8 -> 0

* fix(checker): refuse a capability policy written twice, in "nish" or as a second "nish"

Review round 3. The manifest reader takes a key's first occurrence, so a
second `capabilities` key inside `"nish"`, or a second top-level `"nish"`,
had its policy dropped in silence. `"nish": {"capabilities": {"deny": []},
"capabilities": {"deny": ["net"]}}` compiled a program that reaches `net`.
Both repeats are now NL3032 whenever the manifest carries a capability
policy, spanned at the second key. The new reader, `manifestRepeatedKeyAt`,
bounds every position it steps past, so it adds no overflow check.

Tests: tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_repeated_policy, tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_repeated_nish

* fix(checker): refuse a policy key written with an escape the manifest reader does not decode

Review round 4. The manifest reader compares keys as written, so a
`"nish"` or `"capabilities"` key spelled with a JSON escape —
`"nish"`, `"capabilities"` — hid the whole policy, and a
program that reaches a denied capability compiled. Such a key is now
NL3032 at the key whenever it could decode to `"nish"` or
`"capabilities"`. Each escape counts as one character that may be
anything, and every other byte must match. An escaped key that cannot
decode to either is read as it always was, and an escaped `allow` or
`deny` was already refused as no key of `capabilities`. The new reader
bounds every step, so it adds no overflow check.

Tests: tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_escaped_nish, caps_policy_manifest_escaped_policy, caps_policy_manifest_escaped_second_nish

* fix(checker): walk every "nish" object for a policy the manifest reader would miss

Review round 5. A plain `"nish": {"noPanic": []}` followed by a second
`"nish"` whose only key was an escaped `capabilities` still linked a
program that reaches `net`. The repeated-key check ran only when the plain
word appeared, and the escaped-key check looked only inside the first
`"nish"`.

The reader now fails closed on the whole path to the policy, whatever else
the manifest says. `manifestPolicyHiddenAt` walks every top-level key and
refuses:
- a key written with an escape that could be `"nish"`;
- inside any `"nish"` object, a `capabilities` written with an escape or
  written twice;
- a second `"nish"` that holds a `capabilities` of its own.

Each is NL3032 at the key. A second `"nish"` with no policy in it is left
as the `noPanic` reader leaves it. Every step is bounded, so the reader
adds no overflow check.

The NL3032 branches that had no test now each have one: allow or deny not
an array, an unknown key, a repeated `deny`, and a manifest that stops
being JSON. A positive fixture shows that a harmless escaped key and an
escape inside a value still compile and run.

Tests: tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_escaped_in_second_nish, caps_policy_manifest_policy_in_second_nish, caps_policy_manifest_not_array, caps_policy_manifest_unknown_key, caps_policy_manifest_repeated_deny, caps_policy_manifest_broken_json, caps_policy_manifest_escaped_harmless

* test(self): regenerate the src/ checked golden for the policy reader

entries.title: credit a panic or process.exit guard in the range analysis
entries.body:
The bounds-check proof already treated `return`, `break`, `continue` and
`throw` as ending a path, so `if (i >= xs.length) { return }` proved the
access after it. A guard ending in `panic(…)` or `process.exit(…)` did not
count, although the checker's reachability test already treats both calls as
terminating. `walkBoundsStatement` now asks that same `terminatesControlFlow`
for an expression statement, so the two passes cannot disagree.

The checks this removes are exactly the ones behind such guards: the
`Map.keyAt`, `Map.valueAt` and `Set.keyAt` guards in `std/collections.ts`
(90 checks across 59 golden cases and one link golden), and eight checks in
the compiler's own `emit-map.ts` and `emit-parallel.ts` behind
`process.exit(internalErrorFor(…))` length guards. No line is added to any
golden, and no diagnostic or `.panics` list in the corpus changes.

Only the builtins count: the predicate asks how the checker resolved the
call (`nodeCallees` is `null` only for a builtin), so a parameter called
`process` or a function parameter called `panic` falls through and keeps the
check. The reachability check gets the same answer, so a non-`void` function
ending in a shadowed `process.exit` is now refused instead of lowering to

entries.title: migrate --unchecked-indexing to uncheckedGet and uncheckedSet with nish --fix
entries.body:
Under `--unchecked-indexing`, every check the flag leaves out of the entry
package is now a deprecation warning of its own, at the site (NL7002):
`this index is unchecked only because of --unchecked-indexing, which is
deprecated`, then either the rewrite or why there is none. Where a
`nish:unsafe` call says the same thing, the warning carries it as a `fix`, so
`nish --unchecked-indexing --fix` states at each site what the flag used to
decide for the whole package, and the program then compiles without the flag
and prints what it printed with it.

A site is a check the emitter writes without the flag: an element access the
checker did not prove in range, the second check of a compound store whose
right side calls something, an unproven `charCodeAt` or `pop`, and every
`slice`, array `set` and `nish:net` buffer range. A proven access is not
reported: the flag records nothing for a check it drops, so its proofs are a
subset of the proofs without it, and an access left as `xs[i]` stays proven
once the flag is gone.

The rewrites, offered only where the result compiles and means the same:

- `xs[i]` read, a number element and an `i32` or `i32`-based ranged index:
  `uncheckedGet(xs, i)`; for `xs[i][j]`, the access to the inner array;
- `xs[i] = v` as a statement, parenthesised or not: `uncheckedSet(xs, i, v)`;
- `xs[i] op= v` as a statement with plain operands:
  `uncheckedSet(xs, i, uncheckedGet(xs, i) op v)`.

Every other site keeps its warning and gets no fix, and dropping the flag
puts its check back, which is the safe direction: an element that is not a
number, an index that is not an `i32`, a store whose value is used, a compound
store whose operands call, construct or assign, the second check of a
compound store, an access in a generic body, a module that already uses the
name the import would bind, and `charCodeAt`, `pop`, `slice`, `set` and the
socket calls, which have no `nish:unsafe` form. Each refusal's wording is
pinned.

While a module lacks a name it needs, every fix also carries the one edit
that imports every name the module's fixes call: after its existing
`nish:unsafe` import's names, else as a new import after its last import,
else before its first statement. The edits are the same, so the first round
applies one site's fix and the second applies the rest. `src/unsafe-migrate.ts`
keeps the import edit apart from the indexing rules, so the `--wrapping`
migration can reuse it for its own names.

`nish --fix` now applies a deprecation's fix too: a deprecation is printed
whatever the flags say, so its fix is always one a plain run would show.
NL9014 ends "`nish --fix` rewrites each site; then drop the flag".
metrics: tests/fix/unsafe-index-equivalence migrated in 3 rounds; flagged and migrated builds both print "zero 12.5 / 3 0 2 2 3 / 0.75 6 44 42 23"

entries.title: fix an index not proven in range with a panic guard
entries.body:
`NL9007` now carries a machine-applicable fix. Where an index inside a loop
is not proven in range, `nish --fix` inserts

    if (!(i >= 0 && i < toI32(xs.length))) { panic("index out of range") }

at the start of the statement that holds the access, with its indentation.
The bounds analysis credits a guard that ends in `panic`, so the check comes
off; `toI32(xs.length)` is the one spelling of the bound that compiles and is
credited in both number modes. An index in range behaves exactly as before,
and one out of range still exits 1, at the guard's panic instead of the
runtime's index error.

The fix is offered only where that holds: the index is an `i32` or an
`i32`-based ranged integer, the path from the statement to the access passes
through no branch (`&&`, `||` and `??` included), loop or arrow, nothing else
the statement runs before its branches calls, allocates or assigns, the
statement declares neither the index nor the receiver, and the module
declares nothing called `panic` or `toI32`. Everywhere else the warning goes
out with no fix.

The `tests/fix` runner learns a warning-only case (`plain-exit`), a case that
names the code it is about (`code`), so a refused case proves it reached its
diagnostic, and a round trip (`stdout`, `run-exit`) that links and runs the
program before and after the fix. A fixed case's code must be gone after it.
metrics: 0 existing IR goldens changed; the guard-if-condition and guard-switch-discriminant round trips print the same before and after the fix, and their out-of-range twins exit 1 both ways

entries.title: read the root package's `nish` field strictly
entries.body:
The root `package.json`'s `"nish"` field is now one object, written once,
whose keys are `noPanic` and `capabilities`, each written once, and
anything else is NL3036 where the manifest writes it. That covers a second
top-level `"nish"` whatever it holds, a `"nish"` that is not an object, an
unknown key such as a misspelt `capabilites`, a `noPanic` that is not an
array, and a manifest that mentions `nish` or carries a `\u` escape and
stops being JSON. Each of these used to leave part of what the package says
about itself unread, in silence or behind a narrower NL3032.

Keys and string entries are now decoded as `JSON.parse` decodes them, so
a policy written with an escape (`"nish"`, `"capabilities"`,
`"net"`) is honoured rather than refused. An escape outside ASCII
decodes to a byte no name contains, so it can only make a key unknown or an
entry no capability. NL3032 keeps the shape of `capabilities` itself.

The reader tests every position against the length before stepping past
it and combines hex digits by masks and shifts, so none of its functions
carries an `llvm.s*.with.overflow`.
