entries.title: HTTP/2 frames, streams and flow control
entries.body:
* feat(net): HTTP/2 frames, streams and flow control

`nish/net/http2` is the server side of an HTTP/2 connection (RFC 9113),
sans-IO on top of the existing HPACK: the preface, SETTINGS and their
acknowledgement, the §5.1 stream state machine, flow control on the
connection and every stream with WINDOW_UPDATE both ways, PING, RST_STREAM,
GOAWAY with the last stream identifier, header blocks across CONTINUATION,
and extended CONNECT behind SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL (RFC 8441).
`feed` bytes, take events from `next` (a request, body bytes a frame at a
time, trailers, a reset, a window that opened, the peer's GOAWAY), and
answer with `respond`, `writeData` and `writeTrailers`. Every connection and
stream error RFC 9113 names is a GOAWAY or a RST_STREAM, never a panic.

`nish/net/http2-frame` reads and writes all ten frame types of §6 with
their size, flag, padding and stream-identifier rules, into and out of the
caller's buffers without allocating. `nish/net/http2-tls` serves the
connection over `nish/net/tls-tcp` with ALPN `h2`, in a slot pool sized at
start-up. `nish/net/http-fields` is the header model HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
share: field-name and value rules, pseudo-headers in order and exactly
once, the connection-specific fields, and the request, response and
trailer shapes.

Every cap (streams, windows, frame size, header list and block, output,
reset budget) is an `Http2Config` number fixed at start-up. DATA and every
control frame allocate nothing; a request's header block leaves what HPACK
decoded in the arena (H2-1 in docs/security/http2.md).

Measured: 0 bytes of arena for 1,000 DATA frames in and 100 out; resident memory flat at 10,152 KB for 120,000 and for 1,200,000 echoed DATA frames; 664 bytes a request left by HPACK decoding (712 before HttpFields reused its lists)
Refs: docs/security/http2.md, std/README.md#nishnet--the-protocol-stack
Tests: tests/link/net_http2, net_http2_errors, net_http2_frame, net_http2_tls, net_http_fields (each with an _f64 twin), net_http2_frame_bad_window, net_http2_frame_bad_write, net_http2_bad_config

* fix(net): answer requests a half-closed peer sent, and keep GOAWAY's last stream

Review fixes to the HTTP/2 connection and its carrier. The carrier no longer
shuts TLS down while requests from a peer that has closed its side are still
being answered. Streams opened after the server's GOAWAY are ignored for
trailers as well as DATA, and a later connection error's GOAWAY keeps the
first one's last stream. Even stream identifiers are idle, the memory of
reset streams covers every open stream, the program's RST_STREAM and GOAWAY
wait for room rather than being dropped, a head's Huffman choice never
lengthens its name, 101 is refused, and `host` is compared with
`:authority` without case.

* refactor(net): one GOAWAY writer, one discard rule, and fewer copies in HTTP/2

The connection writes every GOAWAY through one method, so the last stream
it names can never rise, and decides once whether frames for a stream it
does not hold are dropped. Its program-side RST_STREAM and GOAWAY answer
H2_AGAIN when the frame did not fit instead of checking sizes by hand. The
connection, not the carrier, knows when a peer whose stream ended has been
answered (endInput). The TLS carrier decrypts straight into the
connection's input and sends what the program answers to several events in
one record. Helpers std already has replace private copies.

* docs: name the H2 frames pull request in the lane table

entries.title: QPACK with the static table and dynamic capacity 0
entries.body:
* feat(net): QPACK with the static table and dynamic capacity 0

`nish/net/qpack` is RFC 9204's field compression for HTTP/3, with a dynamic
table of capacity 0: the 99-entry static table of Appendix A, the §4.1.1
prefixed integer up to 62 bits, the §4.1.2 string literal with an N-bit
prefix, and every field-line representation under a Required Insert Count of
0. `QpackEncoder` writes a section that begins `00 00` and references the
static table alone; `QpackDecoder` answers a section's fields as windows into
its own `bytes`, reusing its arrays from section to section so that a
connection stops allocating once it has seen its largest section (WP34 N9).
The Huffman code is imported from `nish/net/hpack`, not copied.

Capacity 0 is enforced with the RFC's error codes, each sticky and each with
a `reason`: QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED for a non-zero Required Insert Count, a
negative Base, any dynamic or post-Base reference, a static index past 98, a
truncated section, an integer past 2^62 - 1 and bad Huffman;
QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR for a Set Dynamic Table Capacity above 0, any
Insert and any Duplicate; QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR for a Section
Acknowledgment, an Insert Count Increment and a stream ID past 62 bits. What
a server must accept at capacity 0 (Set Dynamic Table Capacity 0, Stream
Cancellations split anywhere) is accepted, and `qpackPushStreamCancellation`
is the one instruction it may send. A section past the decoder's
SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE answers `QPACK_SECTION_TOO_LARGE`, which is
not fatal.

Measured: Arena.used() moves 0 bytes over 1,000 passes of decoding two
sections and encoding one, after a first pass
Refs: RFC 9204 Appendix A, B.1-B.5; docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md §5 (R1)
Tests: tests/link/net_qpack, net_qpack_f64, net_qpack_bad_window,
net_qpack_bad_field_window, net_qpack_bad_limit, net_qpack_bad_stream_id

* test(net): declare the QPACK programs to nish-cmp

The released compiler's std/ has no nish/net/qpack, so each new
net_qpack program is a declared difference.

* refactor(net): simplify the QPACK decoder and its tests

One tail records every field line, so the indexed form no longer repeats
the size check; the bounds guard, the integer-failure reason and the byte
copy are one helper each; static names that repeat share a switch arm; a
never-indexed field stops the static search at its first name match; and
the tests use the hex helpers tests/link/crypto_x509/hex.ts already has.

* build(std): list nish/net/qpack among the std modules

tests/run.js holds src/std-modules.ts's literal list to what std/ has.

* docs(net): name QPACK's pull request in the WP34 lane table

* fix(net): hold QPACK strings to the field-section limit before decoding them

The decoder compared a field with `maxFieldSectionSize` only after its
strings were in `bytes`, so one Huffman literal of N coded bytes grew the
decoder's retained arrays to about 8N/5 whatever the limit was. A section now
carries a byte budget, and every append is checked against it first: a
static name or value by its length, a raw string by its length, and a Huffman
string by 8/5 of its length or, when that could pass the budget, by the
symbols counted from `nish/net/hpack`'s canonical tables. A section past the
limit answers `QPACK_SECTION_TOO_LARGE` with nothing appended.

Measured: a 1,600-byte value Huffman-coded in 1,000 bytes against a limit of
64 grew Arena.used() by 4,080 bytes before, and by 0 now
Tests: tests/link/net_qpack (limitChecks)

* fix(net): saturate QPACK's instruction counters and test every window check

`capacityInstructions` and `cancellations` counted legal one-byte
instructions from the peer in an `i32`, so about 2^31 of them overflowed it,
which in Nish is a checked panic: a peer could end the process by sending
`0x20` long enough. Both counts now stop at 2^31 - 1.

Each of `qpackCheckWindow`'s five callers now has a case that panics through
it: an encoder value window, an encoder-stream window and a decoder-stream
window join the section and name windows already covered.

Tests: tests/link/net_qpack, net_qpack_bad_value_window,
net_qpack_bad_encoder_stream_window, net_qpack_bad_decoder_stream_window

entries.title: the HTTP/1.1 server on nish:net
entries.body:
This adds a streaming HTTP/1.1 server on `nish:net`, over plain TCP and over TLS, built on the existing incremental parser. It supports keep-alive and pipelining, carries request and response bodies a chunk at a time in either framing, and hands `Upgrade: websocket` to `nish/net/websocket` on the same slot. Every cap is a number fixed at start-up.

**`nish/net/http1-server`** is new. `Http1Connection` is sans-IO, like `Http2Connection`: the program calls `feed`, then `next()` answers `H1_REQUEST`, `H1_BODY`, `H1_END`, `H1_WRITE`, `H1_WS_MESSAGE`, `H1_WS_CLOSE` or the final `H1_ERROR`. The program replies with `respond`, `write` and `end`, or with `acceptWebSocket`, `sendFrame` and `closeWebSocket` on an upgraded slot.

- One exchange runs at a time, so pipelined responses go out in order.
- A `write` takes what fits in the output and back-pressures the rest.
- The framing field and `Connection` belong to the server, not the program.
- Every parser refusal is answered with its status and `Connection: close`. That includes the request-smuggling shapes of RFC 9112 §6.

Two slot pools carry the connection: `Http1Server` on plain TCP, and `Http1TlsServer` on `nish/net/tls-tcp`. The TLS pool serves ALPN `http/1.1` or none, and shuts down `h2` with `close_notify`. Both pools have `expire(now)` for the idle timeout. The constructor refuses a cap whose buffer a peer could outgrow: `maxMessage` above 2^30 − 14, or `maxTarget + maxHeaderBytes` above 2^30 − 44.

**`nish/net/http1`** keeps each head as spans in a buffer it reuses, so a parser with `keepText` off allocates nothing per request. It also adds `maxChunk`, `restart()`, and the writers `http1WriteResponseHead`, `http1WriteChunk` and `http1WriteLastChunk`.

**`nish/net/websocket`** gains `websocketWriteFrame`, `websocketFrameSize` and `WsDecoder.reset()`.

The security record is `docs/security/http1.md`, with three open findings:
- H1-1 (Medium): no deadline for a whole head.
- H1-2 (Low): no lingering close.
- H1-3 (Low): 58 B of arena per accepted WebSocket.
metrics: 0 bytes of Arena.used() over 100 GETs and 100 chunked POSTs on a warmed plain slot, and 50 of each on a warmed TLS slot; 58 bytes per accepted WebSocket upgrade; a 2 MiB body each way through a 4 KiB chunk and an 8 KiB output

entries.title: QUIC streams, DATAGRAM frames and GSO batching
entries.body:
This adds QUIC streams both ways, RFC 9221 DATAGRAM frames, GSO send batching, and a connection that allocates nothing per packet, which closes QUIC-3. It builds on Q3's loss recovery.

**`nish/net/quic-stream`** is new: the streams of one connection, sans-IO.

- Stream IDs and their four types (RFC 9000 §2.1). A client stream opens every lower one of its type (§3.2).
- The send and receive state machines of §3.
- One slot per stream that may be open at once. Each has a fixed receive buffer and send buffer, is found by ID through a hash index, and is taken from a free-slot stack, so opening a stream costs O(1).
- Reassembly in any order. Bytes stay in the send buffer until acknowledged.
- Flow control at both levels, with MAX_STREAM_DATA, MAX_DATA, the *_BLOCKED frames and MAX_STREAMS.
- STOP_SENDING answered with RESET_STREAM.
- The refusals STREAM_STATE_ERROR, STREAM_LIMIT_ERROR, FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR and FINAL_SIZE_ERROR.

On `QuicConnection`, the application's surface is `nextStreamEvent`, `openStream`, `streamRead`, `streamWrite`, `streamReset` and `streamStopSending`.

**DATAGRAM frames** (RFC 9221):

- types 0x30 and 0x31, offered through `max_datagram_frame_size`;
- refused with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION when not offered or when larger than offered;
- sent only within the congestion window, and never sent again;
- `sendDatagram`, `readDatagram` and `maxDatagramPayload` over fixed rings (`nish/net/quic-datagram`).

**GSO.** `quicListenerTakeFlight` writes a paced flight back to back for one `UDP_SEGMENT` send, charging the pacer datagram by datagram. `quicListenerReceiveSegments` hands a GRO receive to the connection segment by segment.

**QUIC-3, closed.** A connection is a reusable slot. The constructor makes every buffer it will use, and `reset(entropy)` wipes the last connection's secrets. Opening a packet and building one each run inside `using _scope = arena()`, which the compiler proves stores nothing.

What still allocates, once per connection and bounded:
- the handshake (TLS-3);
- a client key update (QUIC-4, capped);
- a replacement connection ID (capped at 64).

The aioquic replays pass unchanged; no byte moved.

entries.title: a TLS handshake that keeps its state in the slot
entries.body:
This closes TLS-3 (WP34 N9). A TLS 1.3 handshake now keeps its state in its connection slot, so after the first handshake in a slot, every later one leaves the arena exactly where the first left it. That holds for every cipher suite the stack negotiates.

**How.** HMAC, HKDF, the key schedule, the transcript, the ClientHello read, the message writers and the AES key expansion all now run in scratch space that the caller owns. That lets `TlsServer` do its work inside `using a = arena()`:

- `nish/crypto/hmac`: `HmacSha256Scratch`, `HmacSha384Scratch` and `hmacCopy*`.
- `nish/crypto/hkdf`: `HkdfScratch` and `hkdf*Into`.
- `nish/crypto/aes`: `aesKeyInto`, an additive change made with the owner's authorisation. Its output is word for word what `aesKey` produces.
- The in-place `tls*Into` functions in the key schedule.
- `TlsTranscript.reset` and `hashInto`.
- `tlsReadClientHello`, which reads into a `TlsClientHelloView` that is reused across handshakes.

**Slot reuse.** `TlsServer` allocates its buffers, transcript, secret pools, HKDF scratch and ClientHello view once. `restart` wipes them and hands them to the next connection, and `TlsTcpServer` keeps one `TlsServer` per slot. `restart` wipes both secret pools, and the AES schedules are wiped by `wipeKeys` and `start`; tests pin both wipes.

**Cost.** Each slot now holds about 50 KB more, as a fixed cost, where every handshake used to add 52,808 bytes. The fixed costs and what still allocates are recorded in TLS-3.

entries.title: HTTP/3 on QUIC streams
entries.body:
Adds HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) on Q4's QUIC streams, in three new modules.

**`nish/net/http3-frame`** is the frame codec, read in place and written at an offset.

**`nish/net/http3`** provides `Http3Connection`, the server side of a connection over a `QuicConnection`. Fields go through `nish/net/qpack` and `nish/net/http-fields`.
- It sets up the control stream and SETTINGS, plus the capacity-0 QPACK streams.
- Request bodies stream in through QUIC's per-stream credit, and response bodies stream out as the send buffer drains.
- It supports trailers and GOAWAY.
- It never sends server push.
- It refuses every §8.1 error with its exact code: connection errors close with CONNECTION_CLOSE, and request errors reset the stream.

**`nish/net/http3-server`** is the carrier: one UDP socket and a pool of slots that accepts only ALPN h3. It routes datagrams by a salted connection-ID index, keeps timers on a wheel, and sends paced GSO flights.

Every cap is fixed at start-up and checked against what it bounds. Every peer-driven counter saturates, and nothing scans per frame. A warm connection allocates nothing per request, and a slot is reused connection after connection. The QUIC handshake itself still keeps 89,288 bytes per connection; that is TLS-3's remainder, recorded as H3-1.

entries.title: WebTransport over HTTP/3
entries.body:
WebTransport over HTTP/3, WP34's lane R2 (`docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md` §5). It builds on R1's HTTP/3 (#470) and Q4's QUIC datagrams (#469), and is what the relay (A1) needs to serve a browser.

The new module `nish/net/webtransport` is a sans-IO layer over one `Http3Connection`. It provides:
- sessions made by an extended CONNECT (RFC 9220) with `:protocol` `webtransport`;
- HTTP datagrams (RFC 9297) carrying the quarter stream ID;
- the session's unidirectional (0x54) and bidirectional (0x41) streams, routed to their session both ways;
- CLOSE_WEBTRANSPORT_SESSION and DRAIN_WEBTRANSPORT_SESSION as capsules on the CONNECT stream.

It is pinned to draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-02, the version Chrome negotiates, with its identifiers checked against `wtransport` 0.7.0. One real exchange with a live `wtransport` 0.7 client is recorded and replayed byte for byte inside `npm test`.

Datagram-only use, the relay's, is `accept`, then `WT_DATAGRAM` and `sendDatagram`. None of it allocates, and each session counts its datagrams both ways so a program can cap the rate.

The layer answers some sessions itself, and the program never sees them:
- 400 for a client whose SETTINGS lack H3_DATAGRAM or WebTransport, or for another `:scheme`;
- 501 for another `:protocol`;
- 429 past the session cap.

Streams:
- A stream that arrives before its session is answered waits, unread, up to `maxPending`; past that it is refused with WT_BUFFERED_STREAM_REJECTED.
- A stream for a session that is gone, or one at or past this side's GOAWAY ID, is refused with WT_SESSION_GONE.

Capsules are parsed in place, and unknown types are skipped. Stream error codes are mapped into the WebTransport range as Chrome maps them. Every lookup is one probe, and the waiting room is a salted hash. Every cap is fixed at start-up.

R1's HTTP/3 gains `Http3Config.webtransportSessions`. It sends SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL, SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM, draft-02's ENABLE_WEBTRANSPORT and draft-07's WEBTRANSPORT_MAX_SESSIONS. The four extension settings are recorded in fields of their own.

It also gains held WebTransport streams (the `H3_STREAM` event with `acceptStream` and `refuseStream`), the new calls `openStream`, `writeStream`, `resetStream`, `stopStream` and `writeDataWhole`, and `slot` and `generation` for a layer above. With WebTransport off, R1's behaviour is unchanged.

docs/security/webtransport.md records five Low findings:
- WT-1, the handshake's memory, is open, as H3-1 is.
- WT-2, no clock, is left to the program.
- WT-3 to WT-5 are accepted.

Measured: 0 bytes kept over 200 warm rounds of a datagram and two streams, over 100 sessions through one slot, and after each handshake across 5 connections through one slot; datagrams of 1,167 bytes each way at a 1,200-byte packet; wtransport 0.7's exchange replayed byte for byte
Refs: docs/security/webtransport.md, docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md#5a-landed

entries.title: wake a paced HTTP/3 slot at the pacer's time, not twice it
entries.body:
`Http3Server.flushSlot` took `quicListenerPaceTime`'s answer, which is an absolute time (`now + pacerDelay`), for a delay. It added `now` to it again, after narrowing it to an i32.

On a clock near 0, that filed the wake about `2 × now` away. On a real clock in epoch milliseconds, the `toI32` wraps, so the wake was dropped or filed up to 24 days out. Either way, a slot the pacer held back slept until its next QUIC deadline, which is the idle timeout once everything is acknowledged.

aioquic acknowledges every packet, which kept waking the slot, so nothing showed. curl's quiche goes quiet once everything is acknowledged, and a 100 KB GET over HTTP/3 stalled at 21,875 bytes. The interop job (#487) found this, and the loopback suite (#489) found it independently. The pacer's time is now taken as a time, in i64, and the slot is filed at the earlier of it and the connection's own deadline (H3-6, closed).

Fixing it exposed a second stall (H3-7). When every byte of a stream's resend range has been acknowledged since it was queued again, `putResend` clears the range and the same scan skips the stream's new bytes. The flight comes back empty, and the slot waited on the client. The carrier now asks for an empty flight once more before filing the slot. This cannot spin: it happens at most once after each flight sent, inside the existing 64-flight bound. The fix at the source belongs in `QuicStreams.putNextChunk`, and is recorded as a request to the QUIC lane.

Measured: a quiet client on an epoch-milliseconds clock, with time moved only to the server's timeout, receives a 300,000-byte paced response whole; a held-back slot is filed at exactly now + pacerDelay; without the H3-7 retry, two existing exchanges fail (the 100,000-byte echo and the 300,000-byte paced response)
Refs: docs/security/http3.md (H3-6, H3-7)
Tests: tests/link/net_http3_server, tests/link/net_http3_server_f64
Part of #463

entries.title: give the minted self-signed certificate the extensions Chrome requires
entries.body:
`x509MintSelfSigned` wrote an X.509 v3 certificate with no `[3] extensions`. The W3C WebTransport text asks for none, but Chromium refuses such a certificate. `WebTransportFingerprintProofVerifier` parses it with quiche's `CertificateView::ParseSingleCertificate`, which returns null when the extensions are absent (`certificate_view.cc:395` at quiche 62826931, Chromium 141). The handshake therefore failed with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED before the pinned `serverCertificateHashes` hash was ever compared. The interop job (#487) found this.

The minted TBS now ends with one constant 34-octet block:
- basicConstraints, critical, with cA FALSE as the DER default;
- keyUsage, critical, digitalSignature only.

quiche requires the extensions to be present and well formed, but no particular one, so no subjectAltName is written. The key, the signature algorithm and the 14-day cap are unchanged. This is recorded as X509-9.

The aioquic recordings that `net_quic_conn_replay` and `net_quic_lifecycle_replay` replay carry the old certificate in their TLS transcripts. So `net_tls_common`'s `leafCertificate()` now returns that certificate as a frozen constant, and the recordings stay valid byte for byte. A new handshake in `crypto_x509` presents a freshly minted certificate with the extensions. The client verifies CertificateVerify under the key it reads back from that certificate.

Measured: OpenSSL 3.0.13 reads the golden with both extensions and `openssl verify -x509_strict -purpose sslserver` passes; the TBS grows from 205 to 239 bytes; the malformed-DER corpus grows from 25,281 to 25,701 inputs, all properties holding
Refs: docs/security/crypto-x509.md (X509-9)
Tests: tests/link/crypto_x509, tests/link/crypto_x509_f64, tests/link/crypto_x509_audit, tests/link/crypto_x509_malformed
Part of #463
